title: Reasoning and Fallacies
bigQuestion: How can you tell whether an argument actually proves what it claims, or only sounds as if it does?

story.title: The Number Was True. The Conclusion Was Not.
story.kicker: A driver hears a real statistic on the radio, reasons from it carefully, and reaches a conclusion that is exactly wrong.
paragraphs: Marisol was driving home on Cicero Avenue when a voice on the radio said something that made her grip the wheel: most car crashes happen within a few miles of the driver's home. The number was real. Insurance companies have reported versions of it for years, and it is roughly true for most drivers in most cities. Marisol did what a thoughtful person does with a fact. She drew a conclusion from it. If crashes happen near home, she told her brother that night, then the dangerous part of any trip is the beginning and the end. The long stretch on the highway is the safe part.

Her brother Dante, who was taking a statistics class at Harold Washington College, asked her one question. Where do you do most of your driving? Marisol thought about it. To work, to the grocery store, to their mother's apartment, to school. All of it within a few miles of home. She drove to Milwaukee twice a year. Of course most of her crashes, if she ever had any, would happen near home. That is where most of her miles were.

The statistic had not lied. Marisol's reasoning had added something the statistic never said. She had silently assumed that people drive the same amount everywhere, so that a crash near home must mean home is dangerous. Take that hidden assumption out, and the conclusion collapses. The fact that more crashes happen near home says almost nothing about whether a mile near home is riskier than a mile on the interstate. To know that, you would need crashes per mile driven, and the radio had not given her that.

Dante drew it on a napkin: a fat bar for miles driven near home, a thin bar for miles driven far away, and then crashes stacked on top. The tall crash bar sat on the tall miles bar. The picture made the mistake visible in a way the sentence had not. Marisol laughed, but she also noticed something uncomfortable. She had reasoned in good faith, from a true premise, and still been wrong. If that could happen with one number on the radio, it could happen with a campaign ad, a news headline, a sales pitch, or an essay of her own.

This chapter is about that gap: the space between a claim and the conclusion someone draws from it. Reasoning has a structure, and the structure can be checked. Some arguments are built so that if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Others only make a conclusion likely. Many arguments that sound convincing have a break somewhere in the chain, and the breaks come in recognizable shapes with names. Learning those shapes is the difference between being persuaded and being convinced.
story.think: Marisol's premise was true and her reasoning felt careful, yet her conclusion was wrong. What was the missing piece, and where else in daily life might the same missing piece hide?

lessons.title: Deductive Reasoning
lessons.mainIdea: A deductive argument is built so that if its premises are true, its conclusion cannot be false.
reading: Read this small argument. All Chicago Public Schools are closed on Labor Day. Lane Tech is a Chicago Public School. So Lane Tech is closed on Labor Day. Notice what happened. You did not need to visit Lane Tech on Labor Day to be sure. Once you accept the two opening statements, the ending is forced. That is *deductive* reasoning: the conclusion is already contained in the premises, and the argument simply draws it out.

A *premise* is a statement the argument starts from, a reason offered in support. The *conclusion* is the statement the premises are meant to support. In the Lane Tech argument there are two premises, one general (all CPS schools are closed) and one specific (Lane Tech is a CPS school). The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle called this three-part shape a syllogism, and he noticed that its power comes from its form, not its subject. Swap in any general rule, any member of the group, and the machine still runs.

Deduction is the reasoning of mathematics and of the law. A geometry proof moves from definitions and earlier results to a conclusion that must follow. A judge reasons from a law (anyone who does X is guilty of Y) plus a finding of fact (this person did X) to a verdict. In each case the argument does not gather new evidence at the end. It shows that the conclusion was already guaranteed by what came before.

The catch is that deduction is only as good as its starting points. If the first premise were false, if some CPS schools stayed open on Labor Day, the argument would still have a perfect shape and a worthless conclusion. So when you meet a deductive argument, you have two separate questions to ask. Does the conclusion really follow from the premises? And are the premises actually true? The next two lessons take those questions one at a time.

words.d: reasoning in which the conclusion must be true if the premises are true
a statement an argument starts from and offers as a reason
the statement an argument's premises are meant to support
a three-part deductive argument: a general premise, a specific premise, a conclusion

look.title: Aristotle on the Shape of an Argument
look.text: Aristotle described a syllogism as a piece of speech in which, once certain things have been stated, something else follows from them by necessity, simply because those things were stated.
look.prompt: Aristotle says the conclusion follows by necessity from what was stated. What does that word necessity rule out, and why does it matter for a reader checking an argument?

check.q: In a deductive argument, what is true of the conclusion if the premises are true?
check.why: Deduction is defined by that guarantee: true premises force a true conclusion.

check.q: Which of these is a premise in the Lane Tech argument?
choices: Lane Tech has a large campus
Lane Tech is closed on Labor Day
Lane Tech is a Chicago Public School
check.why: That statement is one of the two reasons the argument starts from; the closing on Labor Day is the conclusion.

check.q: Why does the lesson say deduction is only as good as its starting points?
choices: Because a perfect shape with a false premise gives a worthless conclusion
Because deductive arguments never have a clear form
Because premises must always be specific, never general
Because judges do not use deduction
check.why: The form guarantees the conclusion only if the premises are true; a false premise breaks the guarantee even when the shape is right.

lessons.title: Inductive Reasoning
lessons.mainIdea: Inductive reasoning moves from observed cases to a general conclusion that is likely, never certain.
reading: A nurse at Stroger Hospital notices that the last forty patients who came in with a certain rash had all eaten at the same food festival. She concludes that the festival is probably the source. She could be wrong. Patient forty-one might have caught the rash somewhere else, and the first forty might be a coincidence. But forty cases pointing one way make her conclusion strong. This is *inductive* reasoning: gathering particular observations and moving to a general claim that is probable, not guaranteed.

Almost everything you know about the world came to you by induction. The sun has risen every morning of your life, so you expect it tomorrow. Every raven anyone has recorded has been black, so you say ravens are black. Science works this way. A researcher runs a trial with two thousand people and concludes that a drug lowers blood pressure in people generally. The conclusion reaches past the evidence, to people who were never in the trial. That reach is the whole point, and also the risk.

Because induction never reaches certainty, we judge it by strength. A strong inductive argument has many cases, chosen fairly, that all point the same way. A weak one has few cases, or cases picked because they fit. Three friends who hate a new phone do not tell you much about the phone. A survey of three thousand owners, chosen at random, tells you a great deal. The difference is not the kind of reasoning. It is the size and fairness of the *sample*.

Deduction and induction work together. A detective reasons inductively from mud on a boot to a likely walk through the park, then deductively from a rule (the park gates lock at nine) to the time the suspect must have been there. When you read an argument, ask which move the writer is making. If it is a deduction, check the form and the premises. If it is an induction, check how many cases, how they were chosen, and how far past them the conclusion reaches.

words.d: reasoning from particular observations to a general conclusion that is probable
the set of cases actually observed, from which a general conclusion is drawn
likely to be true, but not guaranteed

look.title: A Detective's Boast
look.text: In A Study in Scarlet, Sherlock Holmes claims that a trained reasoner, shown a single drop of water, could work out the possibility of an ocean or a great waterfall without ever having seen one. Dr. Watson, reading this, thinks it is nonsense until Holmes reads Watson's own history from his tan and his stiff arm.
look.cite: Arthur Conan Doyle, A Study in Scarlet, 1887 (described, not quoted)
look.prompt: Holmes reasons from a few small clues to a large conclusion. Is that reasoning deductive or inductive, and what would make his conclusion weak rather than strong?

check.q: What separates a strong inductive argument from a weak one?
choices: Whether it has a general premise
The size and fairness of its sample
check.why: Induction is judged by strength, and strength comes from many fairly chosen cases pointing the same way.

check.q: The nurse concludes the festival is probably the source of the rash. Why can she not be certain?
choices: Because forty cases is too few to matter
Because inductive conclusions reach past the observed cases
Because hospitals do not use reasoning
check.why: Her conclusion covers patients she has not seen; induction always extends beyond its evidence, so it can be strong but never guaranteed.

check.q: Which of these is an inductive move?
choices: The gates lock at nine, so anyone inside after nine was locked in
All squares have four sides, so this square has four sides
Every recorded raven has been black, so ravens are black
If it rains, the game is off; it is raining; the game is off
check.why: It moves from observed cases to a general claim; the others draw conclusions already contained in their premises.

lessons.title: Valid, Sound, or Neither
lessons.mainIdea: A valid argument has the right form; a sound argument has the right form and true premises.
reading: Here is an argument with a perfect shape and a rotten start. All fish can fly. A trout is a fish. Therefore a trout can fly. Laugh, but look closely: if the first two sentences were true, the third would have to be. Logicians call an argument like this *valid*. Validity is about form only. It asks whether the conclusion follows from the premises, and it does not care whether the premises are true.

Now here is an argument with true sentences and a broken shape. All dogs are mammals. All cats are mammals. Therefore all dogs are cats. Every premise is true, and the conclusion is false, which proves the form is bad. Being a mammal does not make dogs cats any more than living in Illinois makes you a resident of Springfield. This argument is *invalid*, and no amount of true premises can rescue it.

An argument that is valid and has true premises is *sound*. Sound arguments are the goal, and they are rarer than they look. The trout argument fails on truth. The dogs-and-cats argument fails on form. Marisol's crash argument from the chapter opening failed on form too: her true premise about crashes near home could not by itself support her conclusion about where driving is dangerous. A premise she never stated, that people drive equally everywhere, was doing the work, and that premise was false.

So checking a deductive argument is a two-step job. First, pretend the premises are true and ask whether the conclusion is forced. If not, stop: the argument is invalid. Second, if it is valid, test each premise against what you know. A good test for validity is to imagine a case where the premises hold and the conclusion fails. If you can build one, the form is broken. If you cannot, the form holds, and the only question left is whether the writer's starting points are true.

words.d: having a form in which the conclusion must follow if the premises are true
having a form in which the premises could be true and the conclusion still false
both valid and built on premises that are actually true

look.title: Sort These Three
look.text: Argument A: All senators are at least thirty years old. Tammy Duckworth is a senator. So Tammy Duckworth is at least thirty. Argument B: Some Illinois towns are on Lake Michigan. Peoria is an Illinois town. So Peoria is on Lake Michigan. Argument C: All birds have fur. A robin is a bird. So a robin has fur.
look.prompt: Which argument is sound, which is valid but not sound, and which is invalid? Explain each verdict using the two-step test from the reading.

check.q: An argument has true premises and a false conclusion. What do you know about it?
choices: It is valid but not sound
check.why: In a valid argument, true premises cannot produce a false conclusion, so this one must have a broken form.

check.q: What does validity ask about?
choices: Whether the form forces the conclusion
Whether the argument is about a real topic
check.why: Validity is purely about structure; truth of the premises is a separate question.

check.q: Why is the argument All fish can fly; a trout is a fish; so a trout can fly valid but not sound?
choices: Its conclusion does not follow from its premises
Its form is correct but its first premise is false
It is inductive rather than deductive
check.why: The shape guarantees the conclusion, but soundness also requires true premises, and fish cannot fly.

lessons.title: The Premise Nobody Stated
lessons.mainIdea: Most real arguments rest on an unstated premise, and finding it is the fastest way to test them.
reading: Someone says: He went to Northwestern, so he must be smart. There is only one premise on the surface, and the conclusion does not follow from it alone. Something is missing. Fill it in and the argument becomes: Everyone who went to Northwestern is smart. He went to Northwestern. So he is smart. Now it is valid, and now you can see the weak spot. The first premise, the one nobody said out loud, is the one that is hard to defend. That silent premise is a *hidden assumption*.

Real arguments almost always leave a premise unspoken, and that is not dishonest. Spelling out every step would make speech unbearable. The trouble is that the hidden premise is often the one that carries the weight. An ad says: Nine out of ten dentists recommend this brush, so you should buy it. The hidden assumption is that what most dentists recommend is what you need. Maybe. A politician says: Crime rose after the new law, so the law caused it. The hidden assumption is that nothing else changed. Probably not.

To find a hidden assumption, write the stated premise and the conclusion on two lines and ask what sentence would have to sit between them to make the argument valid. Then ask whether that sentence is true. Marisol's crash argument worked this way. Stated premise: most crashes happen near home. Conclusion: driving near home is more dangerous. The bridge sentence: people drive the same number of miles everywhere. False, so the bridge collapses.

This tool cuts both ways. When you write, your own arguments carry hidden assumptions, and a sharp reader will find them. Before you turn in an essay, do the two-line test on your main claim. If the bridge sentence is something your reader would accept without a fight, leave it silent. If it is the very thing a reader might doubt, you have found the paragraph you still need to write.

words.d: an unstated premise an argument needs in order to reach its conclusion
the sentence that would have to be true to connect a stated premise to its conclusion
to give reasons showing a claim is true when it is challenged

look.title: Find the Bridge
look.text: Three arguments overheard in one day. One: This restaurant has a line out the door, so the food must be good. Two: She did not answer my text, so she is angry at me. Three: The Bears won their last four games, so they will win on Sunday.
look.prompt: For each argument, write the bridge sentence that would make it valid. Which of the three bridges would you be least willing to sign your name to, and why?

check.q: What is a hidden assumption?
choices: A conclusion the writer refuses to state
A fact the reader already knows
A premise that is false on purpose
An unstated premise the argument needs
check.why: It is the silent step that connects the stated premise to the conclusion.

check.q: In the ad about nine out of ten dentists, what is the hidden assumption?
choices: What most dentists recommend is what you need
Dentists are paid by the company
Nine out of ten is a small number
check.why: The stated fact about dentists only supports buying the brush if you assume their recommendation fits your needs.

check.q: Why does the lesson say leaving a premise unspoken is not always dishonest?
choices: Because stating every step would make speech unbearable
Because hidden premises are always true
Because writers are not responsible for their assumptions
check.why: Everyday arguments skip steps that any reader would grant; the problem comes only when the skipped step is the doubtful one.

lessons.title: Four Kinds of Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Anecdote, statistic, expert testimony and analogy each support a claim in a different way and each has a built-in limit.
reading: Suppose the claim is that later school start times help teenagers. Four writers support it four ways. The first tells the story of her cousin, who slept an hour more and raised his grades. That is an *anecdote*: one case, told vividly. It is powerful because it is human and specific. Its limit is that one case proves nothing about the rest. The cousin might have raised his grades for ten other reasons, and a different cousin might have done worse.

The second writer cites a study of nine thousand students across eight schools in which later start times were followed by higher attendance. That is a *statistic*: a number drawn from many cases. Its strength is breadth. Its limits are the questions it invites. Who was counted? How were the schools chosen? Did anything else change at the same time? A statistic answers one question precisely and can be quietly stretched to answer questions it never asked, as Marisol found.

The third quotes a sleep researcher from the University of Chicago who says teenage bodies are wired to fall asleep late. That is *expert testimony*. It matters because the expert has seen more evidence than you have. Its limit is that experts can be wrong, can speak outside their field, and can disagree with each other. A researcher on sleep is worth hearing about sleep, not about bus schedules or budgets. The fourth writer argues that we would never schedule a night-shift worker's most important meeting at three in the morning, so why schedule a teenager's hardest class at seven. That is an *analogy*: a comparison that says two situations are alike in the way that matters. It illuminates, but it proves only as much as the two cases truly share.

A strong argument uses more than one kind and matches each to its job. An anecdote opens a door; a statistic shows the door is not the only one; an expert explains what is behind it; an analogy helps a reader who has never walked through. When you evaluate someone else's evidence, name the kind first. Then ask the limiting question that belongs to that kind. Does this one case stand for many? What exactly was counted? Is this expert in the right field? Are these two things alike where it counts?

words.d: a single specific case told as a story and offered as evidence
a number summarizing many cases, such as a rate or an average
the judgment of a person with special training or knowledge in the relevant field
a comparison claiming two situations are alike in the way that matters

look.title: One Claim, Four Supports
look.text: Claim: the city should plant more trees along Chicago streets. Support one: my block got trees in 2019 and summers feel cooler now. Support two: a survey of two hundred blocks found tree-lined streets averaged several degrees cooler on hot afternoons. Support three: a forestry professor says shade lowers pavement temperature. Support four: a tree is like an umbrella the whole block shares.
look.prompt: Name the kind of evidence in each support, then write the limiting question a careful reader should ask of each one.

check.q: What is the built-in limit of an anecdote?
choices: It is too hard to understand
One case proves nothing about the rest
check.why: An anecdote is a single case; it can open a door but cannot by itself show a pattern.

check.q: A sleep researcher is quoted about school bus budgets. Which limiting question applies?
choices: Is this expert speaking in the right field?
Are these two situations really alike?
Does this one story stand for many?
check.why: Expert testimony carries weight only inside the expert's field; budgets are outside a sleep researcher's expertise.

check.q: Why does the lesson recommend using more than one kind of evidence?
choices: Because each kind does a different job and covers another's limit
Because readers cannot follow a single kind
Because analogies replace all other evidence
check.why: An anecdote humanizes, a statistic shows breadth, an expert explains, an analogy clarifies; together they cover one another's weaknesses.

lessons.title: Reading Numbers Honestly
lessons.mainIdea: A statistic or graph answers a precise question, and the reader's job is to find out which one.
reading: A headline reads: Shark attacks double in a year. Alarming, until you learn the count went from two to four. Another reads: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together every summer. True, and ice cream does not cause drowning; hot weather sends people to both the freezer and the lake. A third shows a graph where a line shoots upward, until you see the vertical axis starts at 98 and ends at 100. Each number is real. Each presentation invites a conclusion the number does not support.

Three questions rescue you. First, what is the *base rate*, the ordinary background level? A doubling from two to four is not the same as a doubling from two thousand to four thousand, and a rate (crashes per mile, cases per thousand people) is almost always more honest than a raw count. Second, is this a *correlation* or a cause? Two things rising together is a correlation. Proving one causes the other takes more: ruling out a third factor, like hot weather, and often a controlled comparison. Third, what does the graph's frame do? A truncated axis, a cherry-picked start year, or a scale that stretches one side can make a molehill look like a cliff.

Look at a small example. A school reports that students who attend tutoring score twelve points higher on average than those who do not. Does tutoring add twelve points? Maybe. But who chooses tutoring? Possibly the students who already care most about their grades. The comparison is between two groups that differed before tutoring began, so the twelve points may measure motivation as much as tutoring. A fairer test would assign students to tutoring at random and compare afterward. Until then, the number is a correlation with a story attached.

None of this means numbers are untrustworthy. It means numbers are precise, and precision cuts both ways. A statistic answers exactly the question that was asked of it, in exactly the group that was counted, over exactly the span that was measured. Your job as a reader is to recover that question. Your job as a writer is to state it, so that your reader never has to.

words.d: the ordinary background level of something, against which a change is measured
a pattern in which two things rise or fall together, which by itself does not prove cause
a graph axis that does not start at zero, which can exaggerate small differences

look.title: Where the Miles Are
rows: Miles driven within 5 miles of home, one month
Miles driven farther than 5 miles from home, one month
Close calls within 5 miles of home
Close calls farther than 5 miles from home
look.cite: a driver's log, written for this lesson
look.prompt: Two thirds of the close calls happened near home. Compute close calls per hundred miles for each zone. Where is a single mile actually riskier, and how does that change the radio statistic's meaning?

check.q: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together every summer. What is this an example of?
choices: A correlation with a hidden third factor
check.why: Both rise because of hot weather; the two are correlated without one causing the other.

check.q: Why is a rate usually more honest than a raw count?
choices: A rate compares the count to how much was measured
Rates do not need a base rate
check.why: Crashes per mile or cases per thousand people show how common something is, not just how often it was seen.

check.q: Students who choose tutoring score higher. Why does the lesson doubt that tutoring caused the gap?
choices: Because twelve points is too small to measure
Because the groups may have differed before tutoring began
check.why: If more motivated students choose tutoring, the score gap may measure motivation; only a random assignment could separate the two.

lessons.title: Attacks That Miss the Point
lessons.mainIdea: Fallacies of relevance answer something other than the argument: the person, a distorted version, a distraction, or the crowd.
reading: A *fallacy* is a mistake in reasoning that looks like reasoning. The most common family is the fallacies of relevance: the reply is loud, but it does not touch the argument. Start with the *ad hominem*, Latin for to the person. A student proposes a later start time, and someone answers, You just want to sleep in. Maybe she does. Her motive says nothing about whether her evidence is good. Attacking the arguer instead of the argument is the oldest dodge there is.

Next is the *straw man*. The student says start times should move thirty minutes later. Her opponent replies, So you think school should start at noon and kids should learn nothing. He has built a flimsy version of her claim, knocked it down, and walked away as if he had beaten the real one. The test for a straw man is simple: would the original speaker recognize her own position in the reply? If not, the reply has changed the subject.

The *red herring* changes the subject openly. Asked about start times, a board member says, What we really need to talk about is the football field. It might be a fine topic. It is not this one. A close cousin is the appeal to emotion, which replaces evidence with feeling: a photo of a yawning child instead of attendance data. Feelings are not irrelevant to human life, but they are not evidence that a claim is true.

Finally the *bandwagon*: Every other district has done this, so we should too. Popularity is not proof. Plenty of districts have made mistakes together. The reverse is also a fallacy, sneering at an idea because it is common. When you meet any of these, do not simply shout the fallacy's name. Say what was skipped. The evidence was never answered; the actual claim was never addressed; the subject was changed; the crowd was counted instead of the reasons.

words.d: a mistake in reasoning that looks like reasoning
attacking the person making an argument instead of the argument
replying to a distorted, weaker version of someone's claim instead of the real one
a distraction that shifts attention away from the actual question
claiming something is true or right because many people accept it

look.title: A School Board Exchange
look.text: Speaker one: Our data show attendance rose eight percent at the two schools that tried a later start. Speaker two: Of course a teacher would say that; teachers want to sleep in too. Speaker three: So we should just let students show up whenever they feel like it? Speaker four: Everyone in the suburbs is doing this. Speaker five: Can we talk about the parking lot instead?
look.prompt: Name the fallacy each of speakers two through five commits, then write one sentence that actually answers speaker one's evidence.

check.q: Which reply is a straw man?
choices: So you think school should start at noon and kids should learn nothing
You just want to sleep in
Every other district has done this
What we really need to discuss is the football field
check.why: It replaces the real claim (thirty minutes later) with an exaggerated version and attacks that instead.

check.q: What is the test for whether a reply is a straw man?
choices: Whether it mentions the speaker's motives
Whether the original speaker would recognize her own position in it
check.why: A straw man distorts the claim; if the speaker would not recognize it, the reply has changed the subject.

check.q: Why is Every other district has done this not proof that a policy is right?
choices: Because popularity is not evidence, and groups can be wrong together
Because only experts can decide policy
Because it is an ad hominem
check.why: The bandwagon counts the crowd instead of the reasons; many districts can make the same mistake.

lessons.title: Leaps That Go Too Far
lessons.mainIdea: Fallacies of weak induction draw a conclusion far larger than the evidence can carry.
reading: Induction is judged by strength, so its fallacies are all versions of one error: leaping too far from too little. The *hasty generalization* is the plain form. Two rude cashiers at one store, and a customer declares the whole chain has terrible service. The sample is tiny and probably not typical. Stereotypes about groups of people are hasty generalizations with a long history and real damage behind them.

The *post hoc* fallacy, from the Latin post hoc ergo propter hoc, after this therefore because of this, confuses sequence with cause. A team changes its jerseys and wins the next game; the jerseys must be lucky. A city passes a law and crime falls the next year; the law worked. Maybe, but crime might have been falling already, or the economy improved, or the weather changed. That something came after is the weakest possible reason to believe it was caused. The correlation lesson already gave you the tool: look for the third factor.

The *slippery slope* predicts a chain of consequences without showing that any link actually holds. If we let students use phones at lunch, next they will use them in class, then during tests, then no one will learn anything. Each step is asserted, none is argued. Real slopes exist, and a writer may fairly warn about one, but only by showing why each step leads to the next. The fallacy is in skipping that work. The *false analogy* fails the analogy's own test: the two cases are not alike in the way that matters. Running a school is like running a business, so let the customers decide. Students, though, are not customers who can be turned away, and a school's product is not for sale.

A last one is the appeal to ignorance: no one has proved this supplement does not work, so it works. Absence of evidence against a claim is not evidence for it. The burden sits with the person making the claim. When you catch one of these leaps, the fix is the same each time. Ask how many cases, how they were chosen, what else might explain the result, and whether each step in the chain has been shown rather than assumed.

words.d: a general conclusion drawn from too few or unrepresentative cases
assuming that because one thing followed another, the first caused the second
predicting a chain of bad results without showing that each link actually follows
comparing two things that are not alike in the way that matters

look.title: A Very Small Sample
rows: Share of the chain's cashiers in the sample, in percent
look.prompt: The customer met two cashiers and both were rude, so the conclusion feels justified. What fraction of the chain's cashiers did the sample cover, and what would a fair sample look like?

check.q: A city passes a law and crime falls the next year, so the mayor says the law worked. Which fallacy is the risk here?
check.why: Post hoc assumes that because the drop came after the law, the law caused it, ignoring other possible causes.

check.q: What separates a fair warning about consequences from a slippery slope fallacy?
choices: Whether each link in the chain is shown rather than assumed
Whether the writer uses the word next
Whether the chain has more than two steps
check.why: Real chains of cause exist; the fallacy lies in asserting the links without arguing for them.

check.q: No one has proved this supplement does not work, so it must work. What is wrong with this?
choices: Absence of evidence against a claim is not evidence for it
check.why: The burden of proof rests on the person making the claim; a lack of disproof is not support.

lessons.title: Traps Built Into the Words
lessons.mainIdea: Some fallacies hide in the wording itself: a forced choice, a claim that assumes its own conclusion, or a word that changes meaning midway.
reading: You are either with us or against us. That sentence has done a lot of work in history, and its work is to hide a third option. The *false dilemma* presents two choices as if they were the only ones. Either we cut the arts program or we raise taxes. Perhaps. Or perhaps there are grants, a smaller cut, a different program, a fee. The fix is a question: are these really the only two? Usually they are not, and the person who framed the choice knows it.

*Begging the question* is often misused to mean raising a question, but its real meaning is sharper. It is an argument whose premise already assumes the conclusion. This novel is the best of the year because no other book this year is as good. The reason restates the claim in different clothes. Circular arguments can run long enough that the circle is hard to see; a paragraph that says a policy is fair because it treats everyone justly has traveled nowhere.

*Equivocation* uses one word in two senses and hopes you will not notice the switch. The law says the government must protect our rights. I have a right to be angry about the new tax. So the government must protect my anger. The word right means a legal entitlement in the first sentence and a mere justification in the second. The argument looks valid only because one word is doing two jobs. A related trick redefines a group to dodge a counterexample: no real Chicagoan puts ketchup on a hot dog, and when you produce one who does, he is declared not a real Chicagoan. The claim has been made unfalsifiable.

Knowing the names of fallacies is useful, and it is also dangerous. A reader who has learned twenty labels can start slapping them on any argument he dislikes, which is its own kind of dodge. Use the catalog the way a mechanic uses a diagnostic list: to find exactly where the engine fails, and then to say so in plain words. The goal is never to win by naming. It is to see clearly what an argument has proved and what it has only claimed.

words.d: presenting two options as the only ones when others exist
using a premise that already assumes the conclusion it is supposed to prove
shifting the meaning of a key word partway through an argument
phrased so that no possible evidence could count against it

look.title: A Paragraph Going in Circles
look.text: Students should be allowed to grade their own essays, because self-grading is the fairest system. It is the fairest because it lets each student decide what grade is fair. And since fairness is what a grading system is for, students should grade their own work.
look.prompt: Trace the reasons back to the claim. Where does the paragraph assume what it is supposed to prove, and what real evidence would it need instead?

check.q: Either we cut the arts program or we raise taxes. What is the best first response?
choices: Ask whether these are really the only two choices
check.why: A false dilemma hides other options; the reader's job is to ask what has been left out.

check.q: This book is the best of the year because no other book this year is as good. What is wrong?
choices: It shifts the meaning of best
check.why: The reason is the claim in different words, so the argument travels in a circle.

check.q: In the argument about rights and anger, what does the word right do?
choices: It is used consistently in one sense
It changes meaning between two sentences
check.why: Equivocation makes an argument look valid by using one word in two different senses.

lessons.title: Claim, Grounds, Warrant
lessons.mainIdea: The Toulmin model maps an argument as a claim, the grounds that support it, and the warrant that connects them.
reading: In the 1950s the British philosopher Stephen Toulmin noticed that real arguments, in courtrooms and newspapers and kitchens, rarely look like textbook syllogisms. He drew a different map, and it has been used in writing classes ever since. It starts with three parts. The *claim* is what you want the reader to accept. The *grounds* are the facts, data or observations you offer for it. The *warrant* is the general principle that makes the grounds count as support for the claim.

Take a small example. Claim: Ms. Okafor's class should get the field trip money. Grounds: her class raised the most in the fundraiser. Warrant: the class that raises the most should get the money. Notice that the warrant is usually the hidden assumption from earlier in this chapter, brought into daylight and given a name. It is the bridge between fact and claim. If a reader accepts the warrant, the grounds carry the claim. If not, no amount of grounds will help.

Most disputes are really disputes about warrants. Nobody argues that Ms. Okafor's class raised the most; the sign-in sheet settles that. What they argue is whether raising the most should decide who goes. Another parent might offer a different warrant: the class that has never gone should go first. Same grounds, different warrant, different claim. Finding the warrant tells you where the actual disagreement lives, which is where your essay needs to spend its time.

Try mapping your own draft. Underline the claim. Circle every sentence that offers grounds. Then write, in one sentence, the warrant that connects them, even if it does not appear in the draft. If you cannot write it, your grounds may not support your claim. If you can write it and it sounds like something your reader would dispute, you have found the sentence that must be argued, not assumed.

words.d: the statement an argument asks the reader to accept
the facts, data or observations offered to support a claim
the general principle that makes the grounds count as support for the claim
a map of argument with claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal

look.title: Same Grounds, Two Warrants
look.text: Grounds: the east parking lot floods after every heavy rain. Person A concludes the lot should be repaved this summer. Person B concludes the lot should be turned into a rain garden. Both agree on the flooding.
look.prompt: Write the warrant that leads from the flooding to each conclusion. Which warrant would be easier to defend to a school board, and what evidence would back it?

check.q: In the Toulmin model, what is the warrant?
choices: The statement the reader is asked to accept
The principle that connects grounds to claim
check.why: The warrant is the bridge, usually unstated, that makes the grounds count as reasons for the claim.

check.q: Why does the lesson say most disputes are really disputes about warrants?
choices: Because people rarely disagree about facts like a sign-in sheet but often about what those facts should decide
check.why: Same grounds can lead to different claims through different warrants, so the warrant is where the real disagreement lives.

check.q: You map your draft and cannot write a warrant connecting your grounds to your claim. What does that suggest?
choices: Your grounds may not actually support your claim
check.why: If no principle links the facts to the claim, the facts are not functioning as support.

lessons.title: Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal
lessons.mainIdea: A complete argument backs its warrant, limits its claim honestly, and answers the strongest objection.
reading: Toulmin's map has three more parts, and they are what separate a strong argument from a bare one. *Backing* is support for the warrant itself. If the warrant is that the class that raises the most should get the trip, the backing might be that the fundraiser rules announced that in September. A warrant without backing is just an opinion about what should count; with backing, it becomes a rule the reader can check.

The *qualifier* states how strong the claim is. Words like probably, in most cases, unless, and under these conditions are not weakness. They are precision. A claim that a later start time will raise attendance in most large urban high schools is stronger than a claim that it will raise attendance everywhere, because the first can survive a counterexample and the second cannot. Readers trust writers who know the edges of their own claims. Overclaiming is the fastest way to lose them.

The *rebuttal* names the conditions under which the claim would not hold, or answers the best objection against it. Ms. Okafor's class should get the trip unless the money was raised by a single donor rather than the students. A writer who states that exception before the reader thinks of it has taken the objection's power away. This is the move students most often skip, and it is the one that most impresses a careful reader, because it shows the writer has argued against herself and survived.

Put together, the six parts form a full argument. Claim: the district should move start times thirty minutes later (qualifier: at its large high schools, for a two-year trial). Grounds: attendance rose at the two pilot schools; the sleep research on adolescents. Warrant: policies that raise attendance without added cost deserve a trial. Backing: the board's own stated priority on attendance. Rebuttal: bus costs are the main objection, and the pilot schools covered them by staggering routes. You do not need to label the parts in your essay. You need to have them.

words.d: evidence or authority that supports the warrant itself
a word or phrase that states how strong or how limited a claim is
the part of an argument that states exceptions or answers the strongest objection
stating a claim more strongly or broadly than the evidence supports

look.title: A Claim With Its Edges Marked
look.text: Chicago should expand its protected bike lanes on major streets, at least on routes where a count shows more than two hundred cyclists a day. Cities that built such lanes have generally seen fewer serious crashes, though where lanes were poorly maintained the benefit was smaller. The main objection, lost parking, is real; on most candidate streets, however, the parking removed is less than one space per block.
look.prompt: Find the qualifier, the rebuttal, and the words that mark each. How would the passage read if you removed them, and would it be stronger or weaker?

check.q: What does a qualifier do for a claim?
choices: It weakens the claim so no one can disagree
It replaces the need for evidence
It marks how strong or limited the claim is, so it can survive a counterexample
check.why: Words like probably or in most cases make the claim precise, which readers trust more than an overclaim.

check.q: What is backing?
check.why: Backing shows why the connecting principle deserves to be accepted, such as a rule or authority behind it.

check.q: Why does the lesson say stating an objection before the reader thinks of it is powerful?
choices: Because it fills space in the essay
Because readers forget objections they have already heard
Because it shows the writer has tested the claim against its strongest challenge
check.why: A rebuttal proves the writer argued against herself and the claim survived, which earns a careful reader's trust.

lessons.title: Judging an Argument Whole
lessons.mainIdea: To evaluate an argument, map its parts, test each part with the right question, and then say exactly what it proved.
reading: You now have every tool in this chapter. Here is the order to use them in. First, find the claim and write it in one sentence; if you cannot, the argument may not have one. Second, list the grounds and name the kind of each: anecdote, statistic, expert, analogy. Ask each kind its limiting question. Third, write the warrant, whether stated or hidden, and ask whether a reasonable reader would accept it and whether the writer offers any backing.

Fourth, decide what kind of reasoning links grounds to claim. If it is deductive, test the form by imagining true premises with a false conclusion. If it is inductive, count the cases and ask how they were chosen and how far the conclusion reaches beyond them. Fifth, scan for the fallacies: any attack on a person, any distorted version of an opposing view, any leap from sequence to cause, any forced pair of choices, any word that changes meaning. Sixth, look for a qualifier and a rebuttal. Their absence is itself information.

Here is the method on a short editorial. Claim: the city should ban plastic bags. Grounds: a photo of a lakefront covered in bags; a statistic that residents use hundreds of millions of bags a year; a report that a coastal city's litter fell after a ban. Warrant, unstated: what reduced litter elsewhere will reduce it here. The photo is an anecdote, vivid but single. The statistic counts bags used, not bags littered. The coastal report is the real evidence, and the warrant it needs is an analogy: is a coastal city like Chicago in the way that matters? No qualifier, no rebuttal. Verdict: the claim may be right, but the editorial has established that bags are numerous, not that a ban here would work.

That last sentence is the goal. An evaluation does not end with thumbs up or thumbs down. It ends with a precise statement of what the argument proved and what it only asserted. Write that sentence for every argument you read this year, including your own. Marisol's radio statistic proved that crashes cluster near home. It never proved that home was the dangerous place. The number was true. The conclusion was not. Knowing the difference is the skill.

words.d: to judge how well an argument's parts support its claim
a final judgment stating what an argument proved and what it only asserted
a short published argument giving a newspaper's or writer's opinion

look.title: One Editorial, Six Parts
look.cite: counted for this lesson, from the plastic-bag editorial
look.prompt: Five sentences of grounds and none of warrant, backing, qualifier or rebuttal. What does that shape tell you about where the writer expects the reader to do the work, and which missing part would help the editorial most?

check.q: According to the lesson, how should an evaluation of an argument end?
choices: With a precise statement of what was proved and what was only asserted
With a thumbs up or thumbs down
With a list of fallacy names
With a restatement of the claim
check.why: The goal is precision about what the evidence established, not a simple verdict of good or bad.

check.q: In the plastic-bag editorial, why does the statistic about bags used fall short?
choices: It counts bags used, not bags littered, so it does not measure the problem the ban targets
check.why: The statistic answers a different question from the one the argument needs.

check.q: What warrant does the coastal-city report depend on?
choices: That a coastal city is like Chicago in the way that matters
check.why: Using another city's result as grounds requires an analogy, and the argument must show the two cities are alike where it counts.

choices: The conclusion is guaranteed by the premises
It is used only in mathematics
It moves from observed cases to a probable general conclusion
review.why: Induction generalizes from cases and yields likelihood, not certainty.

review.q: An argument is valid and all its premises are true. What is it?
review.why: Sound means valid form plus true premises.

review.q: What was the hidden assumption in Marisol's crash argument?
choices: People drive the same number of miles everywhere
review.why: Only if driving were spread evenly would more crashes near home mean a mile near home is riskier.

review.q: Which evidence type is a comparison claiming two situations are alike in the way that matters?
review.why: An analogy argues from likeness; it proves only as much as the two cases truly share.

review.q: A team changes its jerseys and wins the next game, so a fan says the jerseys caused the win. Which fallacy?
review.why: Post hoc mistakes coming after for being caused by.

review.q: Which reply is a red herring?
choices: You just want to sleep in
Since we are talking about start times, let us discuss the football field instead
So you want school to start at noon
review.why: It changes the subject openly rather than addressing the argument.

review.q: In the Toulmin model, which part answers the strongest objection or states exceptions?
review.why: The rebuttal names conditions under which the claim would not hold and answers objections.

review.q: A graph's vertical axis runs from 98 to 100 and a line appears to soar. What should a reader do?
choices: Accept the trend, since the numbers are real
Check the axis and ask how large the change really is
review.why: A truncated axis can make a tiny change look dramatic; the numbers may be true but the frame misleads.
